# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it. This is the registered 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial, together with 14 Halden organisations that have record-based output. It reports:

- **Case-processing offices:** the per-hour gain fell from 12.5% at nine months to 9.8% on timesheets, and to 8.5% on the stricter system-log measure. The 95% CI is 3.4 to 13.8. Output per employee is −3.4%, not significantly different from zero.
- **Mediation:** a registered analysis attributes 47% of the gain to fewer meetings and 18% to lower fatigue, leaving 35% unexplained.
- **Counter offices:** the arm was ended at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and restoring service was projected to raise cost per contact by about 9%.
- **Halden:** 3 of the 14 organisations reverted. The 11 that continued show +11.8% per actual hour, which the authors present as an upper bound for organisations that chose reduced hours and stayed with it.
- **Earlier claims:** the report rejects "entirely an artifact." It also shows that the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours.

The arithmetic checks out:

- 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%, and 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8%.
- 34.9/40.3 is −13.4%, and 96.8/86.6 is +11.8%.
- The difference-in-differences on meetings is −3.3 hours, which matches the nine-month figure.

## What this settles

- **The per-hour gain is real and lasts at least two years in this setting.** It is about +8.5% under randomisation, record-based output and log-measured hours, with a CI that excludes zero. This meets every standard Varga and Holm recommended except multiple sites. "Entirely an artifact" can now be treated as refuted.
- **The gain shrinks over time.** It fell about a fifth on the like-for-like timesheet measure, though see point 1 below. Neither "no decay" nor "back to zero by month ten" survives. The point in section 5 about the meta-analysis was checked against its supplementary table, and it is correct and decisive: the four long studies cannot speak to decay.
- **Timesheets slightly understated hours worked,** so earlier per-hour figures were somewhat high, as suspected.
- **Coverage-bound work:** reduced hours cost service, or else cost money to fix. The nine-month waiting-time figures had no control comparison; the 7.3 vs 4.0 figure now does.
- **Meetings matter.** The meetings pathway was dismissed as post hoc. It now has a registered test, with baseline measurement (7.4 vs 7.2 hours, so the arms were balanced). The nine-month report treated it as an open question and this test addresses it directly.

## Issues

**1. The two control offices that cut meetings bias the decline estimate upward.** From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings and improved output per hour by 4.1%. That moves the control mean up by roughly 1 point, which narrows the treated–control gap by the same amount. Part of the drop from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore come from controls improving, not from the treated offices' gain fading. Two checks would separate these:

- Report the 24-month estimate excluding those two offices.
- Report the treated offices' own trajectory.

This contamination also changes what the trial is comparing. After month 15, it is no longer reduced hours against business as usual.

**2. Two time points can't show whether the decline has levelled off.** For durability, the key question is whether the gain has stabilised near 8–10% or is still falling. The report rightly criticises extrapolating two points of Halden energy data, and the same objection applies to 9 and 24 months. The case-management system produces monthly output, so a trajectory, or estimates at 12 and 18 months, could be reported now.

**3. What do "system log" hours include, and is there a log baseline?** Two things need stating:

- **Contents.** If logs count time logged in, including during meetings, they measure total working time. If they count only active case work, they mostly exclude meetings, and output per log-hour then means something quite different for the mediation analysis.
- **Baseline.** The log measure was added for the follow-up, but the −11% is a difference-in-differences. If baseline log data were extracted from history, say so. If the comparison is log hours at 24 months against timesheet hours at baseline, it mixes two measures.

**4. The mediation result needs reconciling with a simple time-composition calculation.** This is approximate and assumes both arms started at about 37.9 timesheet hours.

| | Baseline non-meeting hours | 24-month non-meeting hours | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated | 37.9 − 7.4 = 30.5 | 33.4 − 3.9 = 29.5 | −3.3% |
| Control | 30.7 | 30.9 | +0.7% |

That is about a 4% relative fall in non-meeting hours against a 3.4% fall in output. Output per non-meeting hour is therefore roughly unchanged. If meeting time produced no output, removing meetings would account for close to all of the gain, not 47%.

The two figures can both be right. Some meeting time is productive, and a mediation estimate based on differences between offices answers a different question from an accounting identity. But the gap is large enough that the report should explain it. This also partly revises my earlier reading. The nine-month data suggested meetings might explain most of the gain. The registered estimate is lower, and the reconciliation would show which figure to rely on.

**5. Mediation inference: the effective sample is 14 offices, not the office-months.** A CI of 28–66% looks narrow for seven treated clusters. If office-months entered as independent observations, the interval is too narrow; a wild cluster bootstrap would fix this. The no-unmeasured-confounding assumption is acknowledged, but it bites here: offices with better managers may both cut more meetings and improve more. "Confirms," used in the Summary, should be "supports." Fatigue's lower bound of 2% means its contribution is barely distinguishable from zero.

**6. The control-office meeting figures don't add up.** If two of seven control offices went from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the control mean should fall by about 0.6 hours unless other offices rose. The reported fall is 0.2 hours (7.2 to 7.0). Either the audits partly reverted by month 24, or the other offices increased their meeting time. A single sentence would resolve it.

**7. The cost of case-processing is still not reported.** The nine-month report showed claimed overtime, and output per employee is now −3.4%. The county has the payroll data to report cost per case closed, which is the figure a decision-maker most needs. It reported this figure for the counter arm but not for case-processing.

**8. Halden.**
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the stated pattern.** It reverted citing *client deadlines*, which is the work type the meta-analysis classes as discretionary. So "all with client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the category. Externally fixed deadlines may be a third type of constraint that the discretionary/coverage-bound split misses.
- **Non-responders.** Nine of 23 did not respond, and reverted organisations are likely among them.
- **Secular trend.** Comparing with a baseline two years earlier, without a control group, also picks up general productivity growth.

The authors' "upper bound" framing handles all of this appropriately.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Status |
|---|---|
| Coverage-bound work: output or service falls, or cost rises ~9% to restore it | Settled |
| Headline gains above 20% are inflated | Settled |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Refuted |
| Discretionary work: per-hour gain persists at 24 months, about +8.5% (3–14%) | Well supported, one employer |
| The gain declines between 9 and 24 months | Supported. Size uncertain because of control contamination; whether it has levelled off is open |
| Meetings are a substantial part of the mechanism | Supported. Share uncertain: 47% by mediation, possibly more by accounting |
| Reorganising without cutting hours captures most of the gain | Open. Needs an arm that reorganises without reducing hours |
| Net cost in discretionary work, including overtime | Unreported |
| Generalisation beyond public-sector case work | Open |

The authors' framing of the open question in section 3 is good: does the hours cut cause the reorganisation, or merely trigger it? That is now the most decision-relevant open question in this literature. Only a three-arm trial can answer it, with arms for reorganisation only, reduced hours, and business as usual.

## Suggested additions, in order

1. Report the 24-month estimate excluding the two audited control offices, and the treated offices' own trajectory.
2. Report estimates at 12 and 18 months.
3. Define log hours and their baseline.
4. Reconcile the mediation share with the time-composition calculation.
5. Use cluster-appropriate inference for the mediation analysis, and change "confirms" to "supports."
6. Report cost per case closed.
7. Add the reconciliation of control-office meeting hours.

I can draft these as reviewer comments, or write a decision-oriented synthesis of all five documents.
